Former U.S. Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall accused Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of attempting to politicize the U.S. military, escalating criticism of Pentagon leadership amid a week of fresh upheaval that included Army Secretary Dan Driscoll's resignation and growing scrutiny of senior personnel decisions.
Speaking on ABC News' This Week on Sunday, Kendall said he had "never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth" and warned that the effects were being felt throughout the chain of command.
The comments come days after questions intensified about stability inside the Pentagon following Driscoll's departure and reports that the White House had reviewed potential replacements for Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, claims Hegseth strongly denied to Newsweek on Saturday.
Newsweek reached out to the Pentagon and White House on Sunday.
Officers Afraid to Speak
As of September 2, at least 20 generals, admirals and civilian defense leaders have been fired or departed since Hegseth became defense secretary. Among the most consequential moves have been the removal or departure of senior generals and other top military officials including Army Chief of Staff Randy George, Joint Chiefs chairman Charles Q. Brown Jr., Navy chief Lisa Franchetti, and Navy Secretary John Phelan.
Kendall, who served as Air Force secretary under former President Joe Biden, argued that Hegseth's removal of senior officers and intervention in promotions have created anxiety among military leaders.
"He’s fired 25, roughly, senior officers. He’s pulling people off of promotion lists. And that effect is rippling all the way down through the ranks," Kendall said Sunday.
According to Kendall, the atmosphere inside the military has become one in which officers worry about speaking candidly.
"It's causing people to be afraid and refuse, and, in many cases, I think he's not getting good advice because people are afraid to tell him things that he doesn't want to hear," he said. "Long-term serious damage is being done to our military."
Driscoll Exit Fuels Concerns
The resignation of Driscoll, who served as Army secretary since February 2025, marks one of the most significant departures at the Pentagon since Hegseth took office. Multiple outlets including Reuters and The Wall Street Journal reported that Driscoll's decision followed months of tension with Hegseth.
Driscoll had emerged as a powerful figure within the administration, taking on an unusually prominent role in diplomatic efforts related to the war in Ukraine and military modernization initiatives. He was also a longtime ally of Vice President JD Vance.
In a statement announcing his departure, Driscoll thanked President Donald Trump and Hegseth for the opportunity to serve. "Our Soldiers, Civilians, and their Families are our Nation's very best, and they have inspired me every day," he wrote Tuesday. "We could not have made the progress we did without the support of Secretary Hegseth. I am forever grateful to President Trump for the opportunity to once again serve my country."
However, reports have linked the resignation to broader disagreements over Pentagon leadership and military personnel decisions.
Driscoll had expressed concerns about readiness and the removal of senior military officers before ultimately stepping down.
Criticism of Hegseth's management has increasingly crossed party lines. North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who voted to confirm Hegseth, recently urged Trump to find new leadership at the Pentagon.
"I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it," he wrote on X Wednesday.
Tillis praised Driscoll as “the right man at the right moment” and said he had helped lead efforts to modernize the Army, particularly as warfare evolves in places including Ukraine and Iran. But he sharply criticized Hegseth, saying the secretary was “creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks.”
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis said, accusing Hegseth of being “intimidated by competence” and of focusing on culture-war issues rather than national defense.
Representative Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican and former Air Force brigadier general, has also criticized Hegseth and said he "would not be on my team."
Bacon's criticism of Hegseth's handling of senior military personnel predates Driscoll's resignation. After Hegseth removed George and other senior officers in April, Bacon said the defense secretary had the authority to make the changes but argued the firings were "not morally right nor wise." He later added that "firing without cause shows lack of character."
Supporters of Hegseth argue that a new administration has the right to replace senior leaders who do not share its priorities and that the military needs to adapt rapidly to new forms of warfare. Critics see the scale of the changes differently, arguing that repeatedly removing experienced commanders can damage morale, disrupt succession planning and deprive the Pentagon of institutional expertise.
What to Know About Hegseth's Purge of Top Military Generals
Hegseth has overseen a sweeping reshaping of the Pentagon's senior leadership since becoming Defense Secretary. Among the most consequential moves have been the removal or departure of senior generals and other top military officials.
Some of the most major dismissals include:
1. Charles Q. Brown Jr. — Joint Chiefs chairman
Probably the most consequential initial dismissal. Trump abruptly removed Brown in February 2025, roughly 16 months into his four-year term. Brown was only the second Black officer to serve as chairman. Hegseth said Brown was an honorable officer but “not the right man for the moment.”
2. Lisa Franchetti — Navy chief
Her removal was historic because she was the first woman to serve on the Joint Chiefs and the first woman to become chief of naval operations. She was among the senior officers Hegseth announced would be removed in February 2025.
3. David Allvin — Air Force chief
Allvin announced his retirement in 2025, well before completing his four-year term.
4. Randy George — Army chief
This is particularly significant because George was the Army's highest-ranking officer and was asked to retire in April 2026 — during the Iran war.
5. Christopher Donahue — Army Europe/Africa commander
A highly decorated combat commander who had commanded Delta Force and played a major role in operations against ISIS. His departure came after Hegseth blocked efforts to extend his career, the Washington Post reported.
With the United States engaged in military operations and lawmakers increasingly focused on military readiness and modernization, further departures or operational problems could intensify that pressure.
Warning Before Midterms
On Sunday, Kendall also raised concerns about the political climate ahead of November's midterm elections, arguing that military leaders have a responsibility to challenge actions they believe are improper.
"There's an obligation on our officers, particularly our senior officers, who interact directly with the senior political leadership to tell them the truth and to stand up to them when they want to do something which is morally wrong, unethical, or illegal," he said.
Kendall, pointing to what he described as weakened institutional checks within government, added: "As we approach the midterms, I'm worried that all of our guardrails are gone."
When asked by host Martha Raddatz on what he would do if he were serving in Pentagon leadership today, Kendall offered a blunt response.
"I couldn't serve this administration," he said.

Former Air Force chief accuses Hegseth of leading ‘culture of fear’ as he Trumpifies the military
Former Army secretary said last week that his ex-boss was doing ‘generational’ damage to America’s armed forces
A former secretary of the Air Force who was stripped of his security clearance by the Trump administration last month accused Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of leading a “culture of fear” at the Pentagon where commanders feared speaking their minds due to the risk of losing their careers.
Frank Kendall III told ABC’s This Week that the Trump administration policies in regards to America’s military were coming at the cost of seasoned military leadership who were either quitting or being intimidated into silence by Hegseth, the former Fox News host now running the Department of Defense.
“In many cases I think he’s not getting good advice. Because people are afraid to tell him things that he doesn’t want to hear,” Kendall said of Hegseth on Sunday during an interview with Martha Raddatz.
“Very good people that I know are leaving because of the climate of fear and because of the things the military is being asked to do,” said Kendall.
His comments come following the resignation of Dan Driscoll, a key ally of Vice President JD Vance who’d clashed with Hegseth for months in his position as secretary of the Army. Driscoll’s resignation was just the latest departure in a wave of exits made by members of top brass over the past year.
Other departures have included Navy Secretary John Phelan and the former chief of staff of the Air Force, General David W. Allvin, who quit two years into a four-year posting. Others including some who’ve clashed with Hegseth have been asked to step down. The secretary has also blocked the promotions of dozens of generals and admirals, disproportionately women and minorities
Those blocked promotions have been a source of contention between Hegseth and Congress. Members of both parties have accused him of damaging readiness and command structures, while the secretary maintains that the moves are part of efforts to ensure that the military has the “right leadership”, without explaining what that means. As secretary of Defense, Hegseth has sought to redub the agency the “War Department” and spread what he calls a “warrior” culture at the Pentagon.
The evolution of the Pentagon under that banner has amounted to a fixation on “lethality”, including new image and fitness standards for troops and a hypermasculine tone adopted by the secretary in his public remarks and statements. Under the same effort, Hegseth has dismantled diversity programs and taken aim at any policy seen as “woke” or supportive of so-called liberal values like inclusion. He has also directed the Pentagon to host religious sermons, including one hosted in February by a right-wing Christian nationalist pastor.
“I’ve never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth,” Kendall said on Sunday.
Hegseth has fired back at his critics even as resignations and firings continue to pile up under his watch and Republicans on the Hill increasingly take aim at his leadership abilities. His spokesman Sean Parnell attacked reporters for writing about a “worn out and manufactured” narrative after Driscoll’s announcement of his resignation last Monday. The secretary has not commented directly on Driscoll’s departure.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis issued a scathing criticism of Hegseth that repeatedly referenced allegations of the secretary’s drinking habits after Driscoll stepped down last week. The Army secretary reportedly felt that Hegseth was creating a leadership void through the combination of firings and delayed advancements occurring throughout the armed services.
“I served on Senate Armed Services for 8 years and as chair or ranking member of the Personnel and Readiness subcommittee. I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” wrote Tillis on X.
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” the senator added.
Driscoll, in his own statement, thanked both Hegseth and Donald Trump. But the Financial Times reported that Driscoll said he believed his boss was doing “generational damage” to the U.S. military.
According to Fox News’s Pentagon correspondent Jen Griffin, Driscoll “brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth's blocking those efforts specifically by firing the Generals who were responsible” before his resignation.
“But it was just clear that…Hegseth wasn’t willing to listen to the facts or the truth, or the reason, or any of that, because of his personal animosity,” the Times reported Driscoll as concluding.
The Independent has asked the Department of Defense for comment.

Ex-Air Force sec warns Hegseth's 'fear climate' is driving exits, 'couldn't serve' under Trump
Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III criticizes Secretary Pete Hegseth amid reports about his leadership at the Pentagon.
“I’ve never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth.”https://t.co/epkMjaaGXj pic.twitter.com/KzBuULRsq1
WASHINGTON, DC: In an eyebrow-raising insight into the slew of leadership resignations from the Pentagon, a former Air Force secretary revealed that there is a “climate of fear” inside the department and accused Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of politicizing the military.
The department has faced a wave of exits, with Army Secretary Dan Driscoll becoming the latest top leadership holder to leave. Driscoll resigned on August 31, following months of internal clashes with Pete Hegseth over modernization and leadership shakeups.
'Fear' environment in Pentagon driving exits
Appearing on ABC’s ‘This Week’ with Martha Raddatz on Sunday, September 6, former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III discussed possible reasons and inside developments behind the several departures from the Pentagon.
Kendall claimed that an environment of fear in the Pentagon and “things the military is being asked to do” are driving people out of the department.
“Very good people that I know are leaving because of the climate of fear and because of the things the military is being asked to do,” Kendall added.
Given that “climate of fear” Kendall referenced, the former Air Force secretary said senior military officers have an “obligation” to “stand up” to administration officials attempting to "do something which is morally wrong, unethical" or illegal.
“I’m afraid they’re not doing that,” Kendall said, later pointing out the ongoing US military campaign on alleged d**g boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, which he called “unconstitutional.”
Frank Kendall led the Air Force during the Biden administration.
Frank Kendall accuses Pete Hegseth of politicizing the military
Kendall also shed light on the political transformation of the Department of Defense, accusing the current leadership of politicizing the military.
“I’ve never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth,” Kendall told Martha Raddatz, blasting Hegseth’s leadership.
He said Hegseth's imposition of his will on the armed services “is rippling all the way down through the ranks” of the military.
“It’s causing people to be afraid and … in many cases I think he’s not getting good advice. Because people are afraid to tell him things that he doesn’t want to hear,” he told Raddatz, referring to Hegseth.
Besides Driscoll’s resignation, Hegseth ousted Army Chief of Staff Gen Randy George in April and has blocked promotions of four Army officers with ties to branch officials he fired.
The Defense secretary also removed six Army officers from two-star general consideration earlier this week, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill.

Washington, D.C. — Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III said Sunday that he could not serve in President Donald Trump’s administration, accusing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of politicizing the military and creating a “climate of fear” inside the Pentagon.
“I’ve never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth,” Kendall said on ABC’s “This Week.”
Kendall, who served during the Biden administration, argued that Hegseth’s leadership style is discouraging military officials from giving candid advice and prompting experienced personnel to leave. He said senior officers have an obligation to resist orders they believe are illegal, unethical or morally wrong.
His criticism follows the resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who left after months of reported tension with Hegseth. ABC News reported that Driscoll had repeatedly warned White House officials about Hegseth’s firing of senior officers and efforts to block some military promotions.
Hegseth has removed or sidelined numerous senior military leaders while arguing that personnel changes are necessary to restore accountability, readiness and what he describes as a stronger “warrior” culture. Critics, including some lawmakers and former officials, contend that the moves place too much emphasis on political loyalty.
Kendall also criticized U.S. military operations against suspected drug-smuggling vessels, calling the campaign unconstitutional.
Asked what he would do if he still headed the Air Force, Kendall rejected the premise entirely.
“I couldn’t serve in this administration,” he said.
